meta.title: Who really said "Give light, and the darkness will disappear of itself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: This feel-good line is pinned on Erasmus everywhere online, but it cites no work, no letter, no Latin original, and is absent from Wikiquote. An unsourced attribution.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give light, and the darkness will disappear of itself'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Erasmus across the internet, yet tied to no work of his and absent from Wikiquote. The evidence points to an unsourced modern attribution.

answer.label: Not verifiably Erasmus — an unsourced attribution
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Erasmus across dozens of quotation sites, but none tie it to a specific work, letter, or Latin original, and it does not appear in Wikiquote’s sourced — or even misattributed — list for him. No primary source connects this exact English wording to Erasmus, so the attribution should be treated as unverified rather than as something he demonstrably wrote.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Give light, and the darkness will disappear of itself.
trail: The line is pinned on Erasmus by aggregator sites such as Goodreads and AZQuotes, none of which name a work, page, or letter.
It is absent from Wikiquote’s Erasmus page — not in the sourced quotations, and not in the Misattributed section either, despite that page tracking many genuine and false Erasmus lines.
No Latin original (the language Erasmus actually wrote in) and no specific work — the Adages, Praise of Folly, or his correspondence — is ever produced to back the attribution.
source.excerptNote: Circulated only in this polished English form; no Latin or early-modern source text has ever been attached to it.
source.rightsNote: Because the wording cannot be tied to any dated work or translation, its copyright status cannot be established. The polished modern English phrasing has no documented author or first-publication date, so no public-domain claim can honestly be made.

author.name: Desiderius Erasmus
author.heading: About Desiderius Erasmus
author.metaLine: c. 1466–1536 · Dutch Renaissance humanist, priest & scholar
author.bio: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam was the leading humanist of the Northern Renaissance, best known for The Praise of Folly, his collection of Adages, and his landmark Greek edition of the New Testament. He wrote almost entirely in Latin and prized precise, sourced scholarship — which makes the modern, English-only aphorism pinned on him all the more conspicuously undocumented.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest documented appearances are undated modern quotation-aggregator websites (e.g., Goodreads, BrainyQuote, AZQuotes), none citing a work by Erasmus.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Give light, and the darkness will disappear of itself’?” Last verified 16 Jul 2026.

misattribution.heading: Why this is pinned on Erasmus
misattribution.intro: A famous Renaissance name plus an uplifting one-liner is exactly the recipe for a manufactured quotation. Erasmus is a frequent magnet for such lines, and this one rides on his authority without any textual anchor.

items.why: Dozens of quote sites, from BrainyQuote onward, credit Erasmus but never cite a work, page, or Latin text — and the line is missing from Wikiquote’s Erasmus entry.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict is not “Erasmus said it” but “no one has shown that he did.” Until a specific work or letter surfaces, this is an unsourced attribution, not a documented Erasmus quotation.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentiment — that adding light is a surer answer to darkness than fighting the dark directly — is an old and widely shared one, echoed in proverbs across cultures. Its appeal is exactly why it travels so easily under a borrowed signature.

What is missing is any evidence that Erasmus authored this sentence. A scholar who worked in Latin and cited his sources relentlessly leaves a paper trail; here there is none — only a clean English aphorism circulating on inspiration sites.
context.pull: An uplifting line and a famous name — with nothing in between to connect them.
